Privilege escalation - credential dumping to domain admin
Lateral movement - flat network to servers and clinics
Exfiltration then encryption of servers and clinic storage

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Probable health-data theft and publication threat.
consequences.Availability: EHR, scheduling and file shares down for days.
consequences.Operations: Cancelled or delayed appointments at several clinics.
consequences.Financial: Recovery, forensics, lost revenue, possible extortion demand.
consequences.Regulatory: Notification to regulator and patients likely.
consequences.Safety: Delayed diagnosis and treatment; medication-history gaps.

PbA.rat: Healthcare is a sustained ransomware target; attempts rising.

Pbx.rat: Multiple weak links (triage, segmentation, backup isolation) but perimeter controls exist.

Dm.rat: Network-wide outage with data theft and failed recovery.

Th.rat: Recovery and workarounds untested; small team.

Mu.rat: EHR and scheduling underpin care delivery.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: malicious macro document leading to code execution (initial vector in E6). AV:L: the document is delivered by e-mail but opened locally (FIRST CVSS v4.0 user guide); AC:L; AT:N; PR:N; UI:P user opens the document; VC/VI/VA:H on the workstation; SC/SI/SA:H because EHR and clinic systems are subsequently affected. CVSS describes the entry weakness only, not the enterprise impact.
SCEN.treatment: Layered: MDR/EDR (I03), PAM (I02), segmentation (I06), immutable backup (I04), patching (I05), IR and downtime procedures (I11), awareness (I12). Residual remains material - consider cyber-insurance transfer.
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Backup environment compromised, preventing recovery after a destructive attack
SCEN.statement: An attacker holding administrative credentials reaches backup servers that share the production identity domain and network, deletes or encrypts backup sets and clinic storage copies, so that MediBec cannot restore EHR and clinic systems within clinically acceptable time after a destructive event.
SCEN.stakeholders: CIO; Infrastructure team; Cybersecurity lead; Clinical Ops; clinic managers; off-site backup provider; Executive leadership.
SCEN.background: MediBec has on-site and off-site backups (E2) but isolation, immutability and restore testing are not evidenced. Exercise evidence shows unexplained backup failures on several clinic storage units before encryption (E6).
SCEN.threat_source: Ransomware operator or other attacker with administrative access.
SCEN.threat_event: Deletion/encryption of backups and recovery tooling.
vulns: Backup consoles authenticated through production directory (Analyst assumption - validate)
No immutable or offline copy evidenced
Restore testing and RTO/RPO not evidenced (E7)
SCEN.assets: CJ6 backup servers, off-site copies, local clinic storage.
SCEN.processes: Disaster recovery for all clinical and administrative services.
SCEN.narrative: Days before detonation, the attacker logs into the backup console with a domain administrator account, shortens retention, deletes restore points and corrupts clinic storage replicas. Failed backup jobs raise tickets that are treated as capacity issues. After encryption, restoration attempts fail or reach only stale copies.
sequence: Discovery - locate backup servers and schedules
Manipulation - retention changes, deletion of restore points
Business impact - prolonged outage and potential permanent data loss

consequences.Availability: Recovery time extends from days to weeks.
consequences.Financial: Pressure to pay ransom; rebuild costs.
consequences.Regulatory: Record-keeping and continuity obligations at risk.

PbA.rat: Conditional on an intrusion reaching administrative level (S1/S2).

Pbx.rat: Isolation unknown; failures in E6 suggest exposure.

De.rat: Partial loss of recent restore points.

Mu.rat: Recoverability of every crown jewel depends on it.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: backup management console reachable from production network and trusting production administrator accounts. PR:H attacker already holds admin credentials; VC/VI/VA:H on the backup system; SA:H because recovery of all subsequent systems is lost.
SCEN.treatment: Immutable/offline copies with separate backup identity (I04), segmentation (I06), PAM (I02), backup-alert monitoring (I03), quarterly restore tests and IR integration (I11).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Cloud medical-image transfer storage exposed, enabling bulk health-data exfiltration
SCEN.statement: An opportunistic or targeted actor discovers a cloud storage location used for medical-image transfer and exports that is shared through long-lived public or weakly authenticated links, downloads large volumes of images and associated patient identifiers, and causes a large-scale health-data breach.
SCEN.stakeholders: Radiology lead; CIO; Cybersecurity lead; Privacy officer; Legal; cloud provider; referring clinicians; patients.
SCEN.background: MediBec uses cloud integration for remote data access (E2). Exercise evidence shows medical_image_export.zip downloaded from an unrecognized IP (E6). Cloud configuration, logging and shared-responsibility understanding are open questions (E4).
SCEN.threat_source: Opportunistic scanner or cybercriminal data broker.
SCEN.threat_event: Unauthorized bulk download from cloud storage.
vulns: Permissive or long-lived sharing links (Analyst assumption)
SCEN.assets: CJ7 cloud image storage; CJ2 radiology.
SCEN.processes: Image sharing with clinicians and partners, referrals.
controls: Encrypted storage (E2 - at-rest only, not access control)
SCEN.narrative: An export bucket created for a referral workflow keeps an anonymous access link. Automated scanners find it; an actor downloads several thousand studies with DICOM headers containing patient identifiers. MediBec learns of it from anomalous egress or from a third party.
sequence: Initial access - anonymous or leaked link
Detection - late, via egress anomaly or external notice

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Bulk exposure of images and identifiers.
consequences.Regulatory: High - large number of affected individuals.

PbA.rat: Cloud storage is continuously scanned.

Pbx.rat: Depends on sharing configuration - unknown; E6 suggests weakness.

Mu.rat: Important but not essential to same-day care.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: storage object accessible without authentication (CWE-284 misconfiguration). AV:N, AC:L, AT:N, PR:N, UI:N; confidentiality only (VC:H).
SCEN.treatment: Block public access and enforce expiring authenticated links (I08); DLP and data minimization in exports (I09); object-access logging to MDR (I03).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Misuse of legitimate clinical, privileged or service-account access to extract patient records
SCEN.statement: A malicious or curious insider, or an attacker who has taken over the over-privileged ehr-sync-svc service account, uses legitimate but excessive EHR access to query and export large volumes of patient or billing records without triggering review, resulting in a privacy breach and loss of trust.
SCEN.stakeholders: Privacy officer; HR; Clinical Ops; CIO; Cybersecurity lead; Legal; patients; professional orders.
SCEN.background: EHR access is central to care (E7). Exercise evidence shows unusual query volume from ehr-sync-svc (E6). The appetite statement requires least privilege and logging for high-risk data stores (E5).
SCEN.threat_source: Malicious or negligent insider; external actor using a service account.
SCEN.threat_event: Unauthorized query and export of health records.
vulns: Broad role-based access in EHR (Analyst assumption)
No EHR access analytics or periodic recertification evidenced (E7)
SCEN.assets: CJ1 EHR data; CJ4 billing data.
SCEN.narrative: An employee leaving for a competitor exports patient contact and billing lists; separately, ehr-sync-svc credentials stored in a script are reused to pull records at night. Audit logs capture the activity but nobody reviews them until a patient complaint.
sequence: Initial access - legitimate account or reused service credential
Detection - patient complaint or after-the-fact log review
Business impact - privacy breach, disciplinary and legal action

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Targeted or bulk disclosure of health data.

PbA.rat: Insider snooping is recurrent in healthcare; service-account anomaly observed.

Pbx.rat: Legitimate access bypasses perimeter controls; no analytics.

Dm.rat: Bulk extraction through the service account.

Mu.rat: EHR confidentiality is core to trust.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: insider misuse is not a software vulnerability. Representative weakness used for the workbook: excessive privileges on an authenticated account (CWE-269). PR:L legitimate low-privilege access; VC:H bulk read; VI:L. Interpret with caution.
SCEN.treatment: Least-privilege redesign and access recertification plus EHR access analytics and DLP (I09); vault and restrict service accounts (I02); MDR use-cases (I03); HR/awareness (I12).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Exploitation of unpatched internet-facing or end-of-life systems
SCEN.statement: A cybercriminal or state-linked actor mass-exploits a known vulnerability in an internet-facing remote access gateway, firewall or web application that MediBec has not patched because of uptime concerns, vendor constraints or limited staff, obtaining remote code execution and a foothold for data theft or ransomware.
SCEN.stakeholders: CIO; Infrastructure; Cybersecurity lead; application owners; vendors; Clinical Ops (change windows).
SCEN.background: Patch delays are documented as a healthcare constraint (E3, E7). Asset inventory completeness and scan coverage are unknown (E4).
SCEN.threat_source: Cybercriminal / state-linked actor using public exploits.
SCEN.threat_event: Remote exploitation of a known vulnerability.
vulns: Patch SLAs and exception governance not evidenced (E7)
SCEN.assets: CJ5 remote access; CJ6 perimeter; internet-facing applications.
SCEN.processes: Remote access for clinicians; online services.
SCEN.narrative: A critical flaw in the remote access appliance is disclosed and exploited within days. MediBec schedules the patch for the next quarterly window. The actor implants a web shell, harvests session tokens and pivots internally.
sequence: Initial access - exploit of edge device
Collection / disruption - leads to S2 or data theft
Detection - external notice or threat hunt

consequences.Availability: Remote access outage during emergency patching.

PbA.rat: Edge-device exploitation campaigns are frequent.

Pbx.rat: Patching lag documented; inventory incomplete.

Mu.rat: Remote access and perimeter serve all clinics.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: unauthenticated remote code execution in an internet-facing gateway (typical of known-exploited edge vulnerabilities). All impacts High because the gateway fronts the internal network. Replace with the actual CVE vector once scan data is available.
SCEN.treatment: Risk-based vulnerability and patch management with KEV SLAs and EOL retirement (I05); segmentation behind the edge (I06); MDR threat hunting (I03).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Connected medical device used as a foothold to disrupt clinical equipment and reach the EHR network
SCEN.statement: An attacker reaching a clinic network (through malware, a compromised clinic Wi-Fi or vendor access) exploits an unpatched or default-credential medical device on a network shared with EHR workstations, disrupting device operation and using it as a persistent foothold, with potential consequences for patient care.
SCEN.stakeholders: Biomedical engineering; Clinical Ops; clinic managers; device manufacturers; CIO; Cybersecurity lead; patients.
SCEN.background: Medical equipment is interconnected with the EHR environment; inventory, patch levels and segmentation are unknown (E2, E4). Patching is constrained by certification (E3).
SCEN.threat_event: Exploitation of a medical/IoT device and lateral movement.
vulns: Embedded OS patching restricted by certification (E3)
Devices and guest/clinical Wi-Fi not segmented (E4, E7 - validate)
SCEN.assets: CJ8 medical devices; CJ2 diagnostics; clinic LAN.
SCEN.processes: Diagnostic imaging, monitoring, device-to-EHR data flows.
controls: Firewalls and IDS/IPS at hub (E2 - east-west coverage unknown)
SCEN.narrative: Ransomware spreading in a clinic encrypts the Windows-based console of an imaging device; separately, an attacker on guest Wi-Fi reaches a device with default credentials and uses it as a pivot that endpoint tools do not cover.
sequence: Initial access - adjacent network (Wi-Fi or infected workstation)
Disruption - device unavailable or data altered
Business impact - postponed procedures, safety review

PbA.rat: Targeting of devices is less frequent than IT, but collateral infection is common.

Pbx.rat: Patch and segmentation constraints documented.

De.rat: Some devices unavailable at one clinic.

Dm.rat: Patient harm from altered or unavailable equipment.

Th.rat: No device monitoring or inventory evidence.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: unpatched embedded service or default credential on a networked device. AV:A reachable from the clinic LAN/Wi-Fi only; PR:N; full device impact; SC/SI/SA:L onward effects. CVSS supplemental metric Safety (S:P) would apply but is not part of the base score.
SCEN.treatment: Medical device security programme (I07), segmentation and NAC including guest Wi-Fi isolation (I06), patch/compensating controls (I05). Residual depends on manufacturers.
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Detection and response gaps allow an intrusion to persist and escalate
SCEN.statement: An intrusion by any external actor goes unnoticed or is misclassified because alert triage, log coverage and after-hours monitoring are insufficient for a two-person cybersecurity team, and the untested incident response plan leads to slow, uncoordinated containment, turning a contained event into a major privacy and operational incident.
SCEN.stakeholders: Cybersecurity lead; CIO; Executive leadership; Clinical Ops; clinic managers; Privacy/Legal; Communications; MDR/forensic providers.
SCEN.background: Two dedicated cybersecurity staff (E3); a PowerShell alert was closed as low severity; unusual logins, cloud downloads and service-account queries were not correlated (E6). The IR plan has not been tested across clinics (E8 MED-CYR-15).
SCEN.threat_event: Undetected dwell time and delayed, uncoordinated response.
vulns: IR plan untested; decision rights unclear (E8)
SCEN.assets: All crown jewels; especially CJ1, CJ5.
SCEN.processes: Incident management, clinical continuity, privacy breach assessment.
SCEN.narrative: Across ten days, four weak signals (phishing, PowerShell, unusual login, cloud download) are visible in different consoles but no one correlates them. When encryption begins, roles, forensic engagement and clinical workarounds are improvised.
sequence: Weak signals generated but not triaged
Dwell time of days to weeks
Detection - by impact, not by monitoring

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Larger breach scope; weaker evidence of what was accessed.

PbA.rat: Attempts ongoing; some will pass perimeter controls.

Pbx.rat: Evidence of mis-triaged alerts and uncorrelated signals.

Th.rat: Detection and response are the weak capability itself.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: a detection gap is a control weakness, not a vulnerability. Representative weakness for the workbook: the undetected initial code-execution vector (macro/PowerShell, E6). Do not interpret the score as the severity of the detection gap. AV:L: the document is delivered by e-mail but opened locally.
SCEN.treatment: 24/7 MDR with centralized logging and escalation criteria (I03); IR plan, playbooks, retainer and tabletop exercises across clinics (I11); governance reporting (I12).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Compromise of a critical vendor with remote access to MediBec systems
SCEN.statement: A threat actor compromises an EHR, diagnostic, device or IT support vendor and uses the vendor's standing remote access or software update channel to enter MediBec's environment, bypassing perimeter controls to access health data or deploy malware.
SCEN.stakeholders: Procurement; CIO; Cybersecurity lead; Vendor coordination lead; Privacy/Legal; Clinical Ops; affected vendors.
SCEN.background: MediBec depends on EHR, cloud, device and support vendors (E2, E7). Vendor assurance, contract clauses and access restrictions are listed as areas to assess, not as existing controls (E5, E7).
SCEN.threat_event: Intrusion through a trusted third-party access path.
vulns: No vendor tiering or assessments evidenced (E7)
Vendor sessions not brokered or recorded
SCEN.assets: CJ1, CJ2, CJ8 and vendor-managed components.
SCEN.processes: EHR support, device maintenance, IT support.
controls: Vendor coordination role defined for incidents (E6)
SCEN.narrative: A remote-support tool used by a diagnostic-system vendor is compromised; the attacker uses the vendor's always-on connection to access the imaging server and pivot. The vendor notifies customers two weeks later.
sequence: Initial access - via vendor remote access
Detection - vendor notice or MDR alert
Business impact - breach and outage, contractual disputes

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Health data exposed via vendor path.
consequences.Regulatory: MediBec remains accountable for its data.

PbA.rat: Supply-chain attacks on healthcare vendors are recurrent.

Pbx.rat: Controls over vendor access not evidenced.

Dm.rat: EHR vendor compromise affecting all clinics.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: supplier concentration is not a single vulnerability. Representative weakness: standing authenticated remote-access channel. AT:P the vendor must first be compromised; PR:L vendor account; full impacts. Validate against actual vendor access design.
SCEN.treatment: Third-party risk programme and contract clauses (I10); vendor access only through PAM with MFA and recording (I01/I02); MDR monitoring of vendor sessions (I03); joint IR (I11). Residual largely outside MediBec's control - consider contractual and insurance transfer.
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Manipulation of patient, medication or billing records undermining clinical decisions
SCEN.statement: An attacker with compromised clinical credentials, or a malicious insider, alters medication, allergy, laboratory or billing records in the EHR or pharmacy system without detection, leading to incorrect clinical decisions, patient harm and loss of confidence in the record.
SCEN.stakeholders: Clinical Ops; Pharmacy lead; Laboratory lead; physicians; Privacy officer; CIO; Cybersecurity lead; patients; professional orders.
SCEN.background: Clinical decisions rely on EHR, lab and pharmacy data (E1). Integrity controls are listed among expected controls but are not evidenced (E8). The appetite statement allows no residual risk that creates credible immediate threat to patient care (E5).
SCEN.threat_source: External attacker (extortion or sabotage) or malicious insider.
SCEN.threat_event: Unauthorized modification of clinical or billing records.
vulns: No integrity monitoring or reconciliation evidenced (E8)
SCEN.assets: CJ1 EHR; CJ2 pharmacy and laboratory systems; CJ4 billing.
SCEN.narrative: Following a credential compromise, an extortion group alters allergy entries for a sample of patients and then demands payment to reveal which records were changed. MediBec must verify thousands of records manually.
sequence: Detection - clinician notices inconsistency or extortion note
Business impact - clinical safety review, loss of trust in record

consequences.Availability: EHR in restricted mode during verification.

PbA.rat: Integrity attacks are rarer than theft or encryption.

Pbx.rat: Requires write access; monitoring absent.

De.rat: Limited record set altered and detected.

Th.rat: Backups exist but integrity verification absent.

Mu.rat: Clinical record integrity underpins safe care.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: authenticated user able to modify records beyond need (improper authorization, CWE-285). PR:L; VI:H; SI:H because pharmacy/lab downstream systems consume the altered data.
SCEN.treatment: Integrity monitoring and reconciliation (I13), least-privilege write access (I09/I02), strong authentication (I01), backup-based verification (I04), MDR (I03), clinical playbook (I11).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: API key or secret exposed in code, logs or configuration enables direct data access
SCEN.statement: An opportunistic actor finds an API key, database connection string or cloud access token that a developer committed to a code repository, left in a log or embedded in a configuration file, and uses it to call MediBec's EHR integration or cloud storage APIs directly, extracting patient data without passing through user authentication.
SCEN.stakeholders: Application development team; CIO; Cybersecurity lead; Privacy officer; cloud provider; integration partners.
SCEN.background: MediBec has in-house software/application development and database staff (E3). API key management and repository scanning are listed as an auditable area (E7) and as scenario MED-CYR-04 (E8). No secret-management tooling is evidenced.
SCEN.threat_source: Opportunistic actor scanning public repositories and paste sites; cybercriminal.
SCEN.threat_event: Use of a leaked credential against an API.
vulns: No secret scanning or vault evidenced (E7)
Long-lived API keys without rotation (Analyst assumption)
API calls not monitored for anomalous volume (E7)
Development practices and repository visibility unknown (Evidence gap)
SCEN.assets: CJ1 EHR integration APIs; CJ7 cloud storage.
SCEN.processes: Application integration, data exchange with partners.
controls: Encrypted storage (E2 - does not protect against valid-key access)
SCEN.narrative: A developer pushes a test script containing a storage access key to a public repository. Within hours automated scanners harvest it; an actor lists and downloads patient export files and queries an integration endpoint until the key is revoked weeks later.
sequence: Discovery - automated secret scanning of public sources
Detection - late, via billing anomaly or external notice

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Bulk access to data reachable by the key.
consequences.Integrity: Possible if key has write scope.

PbA.rat: Secret leakage is common where development occurs; MediBec's development footprint is uncertain.

Pbx.rat: No vault, scanning or rotation evidenced.

Dm.rat: Key with broad EHR or storage scope.

Mu.rat: Integrations support EHR and image exchange.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: hard-coded credential (CWE-798). AT:P the attacker must first obtain the leaked secret; PR:N once held, no further privileges needed; VC:H data access; VI:L limited write scope.
SCEN.treatment: Secret scanning in repositories and pipelines, central vault with short-lived tokens and rotation (I14); API anomaly monitoring (I03); scoped cloud keys (I08).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Clinic Wi-Fi compromise or rogue access point gives access to the clinical network
SCEN.statement: An attacker in or near a clinic exploits weak wireless security, an unsegmented guest network or a rogue access point to join the clinic network, intercept credentials and reach EHR workstations and local storage.
SCEN.stakeholders: Clinic managers; Infrastructure team; Cybersecurity lead; patients and visitors; Clinical Ops.
SCEN.background: Wireless and guest networks are an auditable area; WPA settings, rogue AP scans and guest segmentation tests are expected evidence but none is documented (E7). Clinics are geographically dispersed (E1).
SCEN.threat_source: Local attacker (visitor, patient, passer-by) or opportunistic cybercriminal.
SCEN.threat_event: Unauthorized wireless access and lateral movement.
vulns: Guest and clinical Wi-Fi segmentation not evidenced (E7)
Wireless standard and key management unknown (Evidence gap)
Flat clinic LAN (Analyst assumption, see S7)
SCEN.assets: Clinic LAN; CJ1 EHR workstations; local clinic storage.
SCEN.processes: Clinic operations, EHR access at point of care.
controls: Firewalls and IDS/IPS at the Montreal hub (E2 - clinic-level coverage unknown)
SCEN.narrative: A pre-shared Wi-Fi key posted in a staff room is reused on the guest network, which routes to the clinic LAN. An attacker in the waiting room scans the network, finds a file share on the local storage unit and a workstation with an open remote desktop service.
sequence: Initial access - weak/shared Wi-Fi key or rogue AP
Credential access - interception of cleartext protocols
Lateral movement - to workstation or storage
Business impact - local breach or foothold for S2

PbA.rat: Requires physical proximity; clinics have public waiting rooms.

Pbx.rat: Wireless controls unknown.

Mu.rat: Clinic networks carry point-of-care EHR access.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: weak wireless authentication with guest-to-internal routing. AV:A adjacent (radio range); VC/VI:L on the WLAN itself; SC:H clinical systems reachable behind it.
SCEN.treatment: WPA3-Enterprise for staff, isolated internet-only guest Wi-Fi, rogue AP detection and NAC (I06); monitoring of clinic segments (I03).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: DDoS attack disrupts online booking, patient portal and communications
SCEN.statement: A hacktivist or extortion group floods MediBec's internet-facing services with traffic, making online appointment booking, patient records access and external communications unavailable for hours or days and pushing volume to clinic phone lines.
SCEN.stakeholders: Clinic managers; Communications; CIO; ISP and hosting providers; patients.
SCEN.background: MED-CYR-10 identifies online services for appointments, records access and communications (E8). No DDoS protection, CDN or WAF is documented (E2).
SCEN.threat_event: Volumetric or application-layer denial of service.
vulns: Single internet egress via Montreal hub (E2)
SCEN.assets: CJ3 online services; internet connectivity for clinics.
controls: Firewalls, IDS/IPS (E2 - not designed for volumetric attacks)
SCEN.narrative: Following media coverage of healthcare, a hacktivist botnet targets MediBec's booking site. The shared internet link saturates, also degrading clinic access to cloud services routed through Montreal.
sequence: Response - ISP engagement without pre-arranged mitigation
Business impact - hours to days of degraded service

consequences.Availability: Online services unavailable; cloud access degraded.

PbA.rat: DDoS campaigns against healthcare occur; MediBec profile moderate.

Pbx.rat: No mitigation evidenced.

Th.rat: Clinics can operate without online booking.

Mu.rat: Online services useful but not essential to care.

SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Business e-mail compromise diverts vendor or billing payments
SCEN.statement: A fraudster spoofs or compromises a supplier or executive mailbox and instructs MediBec finance staff to change bank details or pay a fraudulent invoice, because payment-change verification and e-mail authentication are weak, resulting in direct financial loss.
SCEN.stakeholders: Finance lead; accounts payable; CFO; suppliers; Cybersecurity lead; bank.

SCEN.threat_event: Fraudulent payment instruction.
SCEN.assets: CJ4 billing and accounts payable.
SCEN.narrative: A look-alike supplier domain sends an updated banking form before a large equipment invoice. Accounts payable updates the vendor record by e-mail; CAD 180,000 is transferred before the real supplier chases payment.
sequence: Reconnaissance - identify suppliers and invoice cycles
Initial contact - spoofed or compromised mailbox

PbA.rat: BEC is among the most frequent fraud types; billing staff already targeted.

Pbx.rat: Verification procedures unknown.

Th.rat: Bank recall possible if detected quickly.

SCEN.name: Lost or stolen tablet or handheld exposes patient data
SCEN.statement: A clinician's tablet or handheld used for EHR access is lost or stolen; because device encryption, screen lock and remote wipe are not centrally enforced, patient data cached on the device or accessible through saved sessions is exposed.
SCEN.stakeholders: Clinicians; clinic managers; Privacy officer; IT support; patients.
SCEN.background: Workstations, tablets and handheld devices support EHR access (E2). Encrypted storage is documented for central stores, not for mobile devices; mobile device management is not evidenced.
SCEN.threat_event: Physical loss of a device with data or live sessions.
vulns: MDM, device encryption and remote wipe not evidenced
Persistent EHR sessions on mobile devices (Analyst assumption)
SCEN.assets: Mobile endpoints; CJ1 EHR data cached or accessible.
SCEN.narrative: A tablet is stolen from a car. It has no enforced PIN and holds downloaded referral letters; the EHR app remains logged in. Loss is reported two days later.
sequence: Access - no lock or weak PIN
Collection - cached files and active sessions

consequences.Regulatory: Breach assessment required; may be reportable.

PbA.rat: Across 10 clinics, some device loss each year is near certain.

Pbx.rat: Some protection may exist but is not evidenced.

Dm.rat: Live EHR session allows wider access.

Mu.rat: Supports but is not essential to care.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: missing encryption of sensitive data at rest on the device (CWE-311). AV:P physical possession required; confidentiality only.

SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Loss of the Montreal hub or WAN isolates clinics from central clinical systems
SCEN.statement: A carrier failure, cyberattack on network devices or data-centre incident takes the Montreal hub or WAN offline; because clinics depend on a single hub without tested redundancy or local fallback, EHR, imaging, lab and pharmacy access is lost at all ten clinics simultaneously.
SCEN.stakeholders: CIO; Infrastructure; Clinical Ops; clinic managers; telecom carriers; Executive leadership.
SCEN.background: All clinics connect via WAN to the primary hub in Montreal where the main data centre is located (E2). Redundancy, alternate site and failover testing are not documented; data-centre outage was screened out in the 10-scenario assessment and is now included as a resilience scenario.
SCEN.threat_source: Accidental/environmental event, carrier failure, or attacker targeting network infrastructure.
SCEN.threat_event: Enterprise-wide loss of connectivity or hosting.
vulns: Single hub and possibly single carrier (Analyst assumption)
SCEN.assets: CJ6 data centre and WAN; all crown jewels dependent on them.
SCEN.narrative: A fibre cut and simultaneous failure of the primary firewall pair leave all clinics without EHR for 14 hours. Clinics switch to paper, cannot view prior imaging or medication history, and postpone non-urgent appointments.
sequence: Trigger - carrier cut, device failure or attack on edge devices

consequences.Safety: Missing history at point of care.

PbA.rat: Multi-hour outages of a single hub occur over a 12-month horizon.

Pbx.rat: Redundancy not evidenced.

Th.rat: No alternate site or tested downtime procedures.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: architectural dependency, largely non-malicious. Representative weakness: denial of service against a single edge device with no redundancy (AT:P specific conditions); VA:H and SA:H for downstream systems.
SCEN.treatment: Dual carriers / SD-WAN, firewall high availability, cloud or secondary-site failover for EHR read access (I18); tested clinic downtime procedures (I11).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Unmanaged patient data on local clinic storage is exposed or lost
SCEN.statement: Patient exports, scanned documents and imaging copies accumulate on local clinic storage units outside central access control, retention and monitoring; an insider, intruder or misconfigured share exposes them, or they are lost without backup.
SCEN.stakeholders: Clinic managers; Privacy officer; CIO; Infrastructure; patients.
SCEN.background: Local clinic storage units exist alongside the central data centre (E2); students are asked where copies, exports and local records are stored (E4). Backup jobs for clinic storage have failed in the exercise (E6).
SCEN.threat_source: Curious or malicious insider; intruder; accidental misconfiguration.
SCEN.threat_event: Unauthorized access to or loss of locally stored data.
SCEN.assets: Local clinic storage; copies of CJ1/CJ2 data.
SCEN.narrative: A shared folder 'Scans' on a clinic storage unit is readable by all domain users and contains eight years of referral letters. A compromised account indexes it; separately, a disk failure destroys files that were never backed up.
sequence: Access - broad share permissions or compromised account
Business impact - privacy breach or data loss

PbA.rat: Local storage in 10 clinics; insiders and intruders both relevant.

Pbx.rat: Access controls and inventory unknown.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: incorrect default permissions on network shares (CWE-276). AV:A clinic network; PR:L any domain user.
SCEN.treatment: Data discovery, consolidation of local data into managed central stores, least-privilege shares, retention schedule (I19); encrypted and managed endpoints/storage (I17).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Web application flaw in the patient portal exposes other patients' records
SCEN.statement: An attacker, or a curious patient, exploits an authorization flaw (insecure direct object reference) or injection weakness in MediBec's online records-access or booking application, retrieving other patients' records at scale.
SCEN.stakeholders: Application owner; development team or vendor; Privacy officer; CIO; patients.
SCEN.background: Online services are used for appointments, records access and communications (E8, MED-CYR-10). Secure development and application testing are auditable areas (E7); no penetration testing is documented.
SCEN.threat_source: External attacker or curious authenticated patient.
SCEN.threat_event: Exploitation of an application-layer flaw.
SCEN.assets: CJ3 patient portal; CJ1 EHR data exposed through it.
controls: Firewalls, IDS/IPS (E2 - limited for application logic)
SCEN.narrative: A patient notices the document URL contains a sequential number and changes it, seeing another patient's lab result. A script later downloads 40,000 documents over a weekend.
sequence: Detection - complaint or social media post

PbA.rat: Public applications are constantly probed.

Pbx.rat: Flaw presence unknown; no testing evidence.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: authorization bypass through user-controlled key (CWE-639). PR:L any patient account; VC:H cross-patient data.
SCEN.treatment: Annual application penetration testing and secure SDLC (I14), WAF with rate limiting (I15), scanning of web tier (I05), enumeration detection (I03).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Trojanized software update from a clinical or IT software supplier
SCEN.statement: A threat actor compromises the build or update infrastructure of software used by MediBec (EHR component, imaging viewer, remote-management tool) and distributes a signed malicious update, which MediBec installs automatically, giving the actor a foothold across many systems at once.
SCEN.stakeholders: CIO; Cybersecurity lead; Procurement; affected supplier; Clinical Ops.
SCEN.background: MediBec runs many vendor applications (E2). Supply-chain verification is not evidenced (E7). Unlike S9 (vendor remote access), this path uses the software itself.
SCEN.threat_source: State-linked or advanced criminal supply-chain actor.
SCEN.threat_event: Installation of a malicious signed update.
vulns: No software bill of materials or supplier assurance (E7)
Limited egress filtering from servers (Analyst assumption)
SCEN.assets: Servers and endpoints running the affected software; CJ1, CJ2.
SCEN.processes: Any process relying on the affected product.
controls: Antimalware (E2 - signed updates usually bypass it)
SCEN.narrative: A widely used remote-monitoring agent receives a malicious update. It installs on 300 MediBec endpoints and servers within hours and beacons to attacker infrastructure. The supplier discloses the compromise a week later.
sequence: Execution - on all hosts with the product

consequences.Integrity: Trust in all affected hosts lost.

PbA.rat: Rare but high-impact events.

Pbx.rat: Signed updates bypass most customer controls.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: supplier compromise. Representative weakness: download of code without integrity check (CWE-494). AC:H and AT:P - the supplier's pipeline must be compromised first.
SCEN.treatment: Supplier assurance and staged updates for critical software (I10); egress control and behavioural detection (I03); rebuild playbook (I11). Prevention is largely outside MediBec's control - transfer and acceptance required.
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Takeover of cloud tenant administration through token theft or malicious app consent
SCEN.statement: An attacker steals a session token or tricks a cloud administrator into granting consent to a malicious application, obtaining persistent control of MediBec's cloud tenant, from which they read mail and files, create backdoor accounts and disable logging.
SCEN.stakeholders: CIO; Cybersecurity lead; cloud administrators; cloud provider; Privacy officer.
SCEN.background: Cloud integration supports remote access and data retrieval (E2); cloud configuration, identity and logging are open questions (E4). Push MFA does not stop token theft (E6).
SCEN.threat_event: Compromise of the cloud control plane.
vulns: Token-theft-resistant controls (device binding, conditional access) not evidenced
Users can consent to third-party apps (Analyst assumption)
Cloud admin roles not separated or JIT (E7)
SCEN.assets: CJ5 cloud identity; CJ7 cloud storage; mail and collaboration.
SCEN.narrative: An adversary-in-the-middle phishing kit captures a cloud admin's session cookie, bypassing MFA. The attacker registers an application with mail and file read permissions, adds a global admin and turns off audit retention.
sequence: Initial access - token theft or consent phishing
Business impact - broad breach, tenant rebuild

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Mail and cloud files containing PHI.

PbA.rat: AiTM kits and consent phishing are widespread.

Pbx.rat: Push MFA and no conditional access.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: session token not bound to device, reusable after MFA (CWE-294-type). UI:A admin must interact with the lure; all impacts High because the control plane governs subsequent systems.
SCEN.treatment: Phishing-resistant MFA and token-binding conditional access (I01), JIT cloud admin roles and admin-consent workflow (I02), cloud posture baseline (I08), cloud audit logs to MDR (I03).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Accidental disclosure of patient information by staff
SCEN.statement: A staff member unintentionally discloses patient information - misdirected e-mail or fax, wrong attachment, record uploaded to a personal cloud, or document handed to the wrong patient - because data-handling controls and awareness are limited, resulting in privacy incidents and patient complaints.
SCEN.stakeholders: All clinical and administrative staff; Privacy officer; clinic managers; patients.
SCEN.background: MediBec handles high volumes of health information across 10 clinics (E1). Privacy controls expected (classification, DLP, breach assessment) are listed as areas to assess, not as existing controls (E5, E7).
SCEN.threat_event: Unintended disclosure.
vulns: No DLP or recipient warnings evidenced
Use of fax/e-mail for referrals (Analyst assumption)
SCEN.assets: CJ1, CJ2 information in transit and in documents.
controls: Privacy and compliance function (E4 in s.4)
SCEN.narrative: A clerk sends a batch of lab results to an outside clinic with a similar name selected by e-mail auto-complete. The recipient reports it three days later.

consequences.Regulatory: Incident register; notification if risk of serious injury.

PbA.rat: Human error is near certain across 10 clinics in 12 months.

Pbx.rat: Few technical safeguards evidenced.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: human error. Representative weakness: absence of outbound data-loss safeguards for an authenticated user. The score is low by design; business impact is captured in damage estimates.
SCEN.treatment: Outbound DLP and recipient warnings (I09), secure referral channel replacing fax/e-mail and data minimization (I19), role-based privacy training (I12).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Interception or exposure of teleconsultations and clinical messaging
SCEN.statement: An outsider joins or records a teleconsultation through an open meeting link, or intercepts clinical messages sent through unapproved or poorly configured communication tools, exposing sensitive consultations.
SCEN.stakeholders: Clinicians; patients; Communications systems owner; Privacy officer; communications vendor.
SCEN.background: Voice, video and messaging services connect clinics and clinicians; confidentiality and secure collaboration are flagged for assessment (E2).
SCEN.threat_event: Unauthorized access to real-time communications.
vulns: Meeting links without waiting room or authentication (Analyst assumption)
Use of consumer messaging apps by clinicians (Analyst assumption)
Communication platform configuration baseline not evidenced
SCEN.assets: Communication systems; consultation content.
controls: Communication systems in place (E2 - security settings unknown)
SCEN.narrative: A recurring meeting link for psychiatry teleconsultations is shared in a patient e-mail and forwarded; an unknown participant joins silently. Separately, clinicians share images through a consumer messaging app.
sequence: Access - reuse of static link or unapproved channel
Detection - participant noticed or not at all

consequences.Reputation: Moderate to high for sensitive specialties.

PbA.rat: Opportunistic; depends on telehealth volume (Evidence gap).

Pbx.rat: Configuration unknown.

Mu.rat: Supports but is not core to most care.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: missing authentication for a meeting resource (CWE-306). AT:P attacker must obtain the link.
SCEN.treatment: Approved telehealth and messaging platform with authenticated entry, waiting rooms, encryption and configuration baseline; ban on consumer apps for PHI (I22).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Brute force or credential stuffing against exposed administrative interfaces
SCEN.statement: An attacker finds management interfaces (remote desktop, hypervisor or firewall consoles, storage or out-of-band management) exposed to the internet or partner networks and gains access by credential stuffing or default passwords, obtaining administrative control of infrastructure.
SCEN.stakeholders: Infrastructure team; Cybersecurity lead; CIO; managed service providers.
SCEN.background: Exposure of services and inventory completeness are open questions (E4); remote access exists (E2). Exposed admin portals and remote management interfaces appear in the extended catalogue (E8).
SCEN.threat_event: Password attack against an exposed admin interface.
SCEN.assets: CJ6 infrastructure; hypervisors, firewalls, storage.
SCEN.narrative: An external scan finds an out-of-band server management port reachable from the internet with the vendor default password. The attacker powers off hosts and later deploys ransomware directly on the hypervisor.
sequence: Initial access - default or stuffed credentials
Impact - disruption, encryption or data access

PbA.rat: Continuous internet scanning and password attacks.

Pbx.rat: Depends on actual exposure - unknown.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: exposed management interface with weak or default credentials (CWE-1392/521). AT:P - success depends on a guessable credential.
SCEN.treatment: External attack-surface management and removal of exposed interfaces (I05), MFA and PAM-brokered admin access (I01, I02), monitoring of admin logins (I03).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Malware introduced through patient-supplied imaging media or USB devices
SCEN.statement: Malware on a patient-supplied imaging CD/USB or a staff USB drive executes on a radiology workstation or device console when the media is loaded, infecting systems that are poorly protected by endpoint security and connected to the clinical network.
SCEN.stakeholders: Radiology staff; Biomedical engineering; clinic managers; Cybersecurity lead.
SCEN.background: Radiology and interconnected medical equipment are part of the environment (E1, E2); device inventories and endpoint coverage are uncertain (E4). Imaging departments routinely import external media.
SCEN.threat_event: Execution of malware from removable media.
vulns: Autorun or unrestricted media import on imaging workstations (Analyst assumption)
No kiosk for media scanning evidenced
SCEN.assets: CJ2 imaging workstations; CJ8 devices.
SCEN.processes: Image import for diagnosis and referral.
controls: Antimalware (E2 - coverage of device consoles unknown)
SCEN.narrative: A patient brings imaging from an outside clinic on a USB key infected with a worm. The import station, running an unsupported OS without EDR, is infected and spreads to a neighbouring modality console.

PbA.rat: External media is imported routinely.

Pbx.rat: Endpoint coverage of device consoles unknown.

Mu.rat: Imaging is a core diagnostic service.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: automatic execution of content from removable media. AV:P media inserted physically; UI:P staff loads it.
SCEN.treatment: Media-scanning kiosk and device control, EDR where supported (I03), medical device hardening (I07), isolating imaging segments (I06), staff procedure (I12).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Retired devices or medical equipment released with recoverable patient data
SCEN.statement: Workstations, drives, printers, storage units or medical equipment are returned to lessors, sold or recycled without certified data sanitization, and a third party recovers patient data from them.
SCEN.stakeholders: Infrastructure; Biomedical engineering; Procurement; Privacy officer; disposal vendor.
SCEN.background: MediBec operates many endpoints, local storage units and devices that store images (E2). Asset lifecycle and disposal controls are not documented.
SCEN.threat_event: Recovery of data from disposed media.
SCEN.assets: Retired endpoints, storage and medical equipment.
controls: Encrypted storage for central data (E2 - not necessarily device drives)
SCEN.narrative: An ultrasound unit returned at lease end still holds 3,000 studies. It is resold; the buyer finds the data and contacts the media.

consequences.Reputation: Moderate to high if media involved.

PbA.rat: Disposals occur every year.

Pbx.rat: Sanitization practice unknown.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: sensitive information in resource not removed before reuse (CWE-226). AV:P physical possession.
SCEN.treatment: Certified sanitization with certificates of destruction, lease-return clauses, full-disk encryption on all devices (I17, I19).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Staff paste patient data into unapproved generative-AI tools
SCEN.statement: Clinicians and administrative staff use public generative-AI tools to summarize notes, draft letters or translate documents, pasting identifiable patient information into services whose data retention, training use and location MediBec has not assessed, resulting in uncontrolled disclosure of health information.
SCEN.stakeholders: Clinicians; administrative staff; Privacy officer; CIO; Legal; AI service providers.
SCEN.background: Health information is highly sensitive (E1) and privacy controls are a priority in the appetite statement (E5). No AI acceptable-use policy or approved tool is documented.
SCEN.threat_source: Well-intentioned insider; AI service provider handling.
SCEN.threat_event: Transfer of personal health information to an unapproved third party.
vulns: Web DLP / category controls not evidenced
Awareness content does not cover AI (Analyst assumption)
SCEN.assets: CJ1 clinical notes and letters.
SCEN.narrative: Clinicians use a free chatbot to turn dictated notes into referral letters. Over months, thousands of identifiable notes are submitted to a service that retains prompts outside Canada.
sequence: Use - staff submit PHI to external AI

consequences.Regulatory: Cross-border transfer and consent issues (counsel to confirm).
consequences.Safety: Possible clinical errors from unchecked AI output.

PbA.rat: Generative-AI use among clinicians is widespread by 2026.

Pbx.rat: No policy or technical controls evidenced.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: policy and data-governance gap. Representative weakness: exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor via unrestricted egress (CWE-200). AT:P - harm depends on provider retention.
SCEN.treatment: AI acceptable-use policy, sanctioned privacy-assessed AI tool, web category controls and DLP for AI sites (I20, I09), training (I12).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Help-desk impersonation leads to MFA reset and account takeover
SCEN.statement: An attacker phones the IT help desk impersonating a clinician or manager, uses publicly available details to pass weak identity checks, and has the password and MFA device reset, taking over the account and accessing EHR and remote access.
SCEN.stakeholders: IT support/help desk; Cybersecurity lead; clinicians; CIO.
SCEN.background: IT support is part of the 15-person IT team (E3). Help-desk identity verification is not documented. Remote access relies on MFA push (E6), which a reset defeats.
SCEN.threat_event: Fraudulent credential and MFA reset.
vulns: Help-desk verification based on knowable data (Analyst assumption)
No manager or video verification for MFA resets
No alerting on MFA device changes (E7)
SCEN.assets: CJ5 identity; CJ1 EHR.
SCEN.narrative: Posing as a physician travelling to a conference, the caller gives employee number and date of hire found online and asks for an MFA reset. The attacker enrols their own phone and logs in within minutes.
sequence: Reconnaissance - staff details from public sources
Escalation - toward S2 or data theft

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: EHR access under a clinician identity.

PbA.rat: Help-desk social engineering is an active technique against healthcare.

Pbx.rat: Verification procedures unknown.

Dm.rat: Privileged account leads to enterprise compromise.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: process weakness. Representative weakness: weak authentication of the account-recovery process (CWE-640). UI:A help-desk agent acts.
SCEN.treatment: Strong help-desk verification (call-back, manager approval, video ID) for resets (I21), phishing-resistant authenticators that cannot be re-enrolled by phone (I01), alerts on MFA changes and awareness (I12).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Malicious or departing IT administrator sabotages systems
SCEN.statement: A disgruntled or departing IT administrator with broad standing privileges deletes backups, disables accounts or plants logic bombs; with a 15-person IT team and concentrated knowledge, MediBec cannot quickly detect or reverse the actions, causing prolonged outages.
SCEN.stakeholders: CIO; HR; Executive leadership; Cybersecurity lead; Legal.
SCEN.background: IT is a lean 15-person team with two security staff (E3). Privileged access management, admin monitoring and separation of duties are not evidenced (E7). Key-person dependency is implicit.
SCEN.threat_event: Destructive administrative actions.
vulns: No monitoring of admin actions (Annex B #115)
Weak offboarding of privileged users (Analyst assumption)
Backups deletable by same admins (see S3)
SCEN.assets: CJ5, CJ6 and all hosted crown jewels.
SCEN.narrative: An administrator dismissed on a Friday retains VPN access over the weekend, deletes the backup catalogue and schedules a script that wipes several servers on Monday morning.

PbA.rat: Malicious privileged insiders are rare.

Pbx.rat: If motivated, broad privileges make success likely.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: insider abuse of legitimate privileges. Representative weakness: excessive standing privileges (CWE-250). PR:H administrator.
SCEN.treatment: PAM with JIT and session recording, separation of duties (I02), monitoring of admin actions (I03), immutable backups outside admin reach (I04), HR-IT offboarding playbook (I11).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Interception or tampering of unencrypted clinical interface traffic (HL7/DICOM)
SCEN.statement: An attacker positioned on the clinic network or WAN captures or alters unencrypted HL7 lab/pharmacy messages or DICOM image transfers between clinical systems, exposing results or injecting false values that flow into the EHR.
SCEN.stakeholders: Laboratory and pharmacy leads; Radiology; integration team; CIO; Cybersecurity lead.
SCEN.background: EHR, radiology, lab and pharmacy systems are integrated (E2); data integrity and application monitoring are to be assessed (E2). Encryption of interface traffic is not documented; legacy clinical protocols are often cleartext.
SCEN.threat_source: Attacker with internal network position (following S2, S7, S12).
SCEN.threat_event: Man-in-the-middle on clinical interfaces.
SCEN.assets: CJ2 lab, pharmacy, imaging interfaces; CJ1 EHR.
SCEN.processes: Result reporting, medication orders, image transfer.
SCEN.narrative: An attacker with a foothold in a clinic uses ARP spoofing to intercept lab result messages to the EHR, harvesting results and altering several potassium values.
sequence: Business impact - wrong results in the record

PbA.rat: Requires internal position and intent.

Pbx.rat: Cleartext likely; exploitation requires skill.

Mu.rat: Lab and pharmacy data drive treatment.

SCEN.cvss_note: Representative weakness: cleartext transmission of sensitive information (CWE-319) without integrity check (CWE-353). AV:A adjacent; AT:P attacker must be on path; SI:H downstream EHR.
SCEN.treatment: TLS/VPN for HL7 and DICOM, interface-engine hardening (I22), segmentation (I06), reconciliation of results (I13).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

SCEN.name: Criminals impersonate MediBec to defraud or phish patients
SCEN.statement: Fraudsters register look-alike domains and send SMS or e-mail messages posing as MediBec (appointment confirmations, billing notices, results available) to harvest patients' credentials, health-card details or payments, harming patients and eroding trust even though MediBec's systems are not breached.
SCEN.stakeholders: Patients; Communications; Privacy officer; Cybersecurity lead; clinic front desks; telecom and domain registrars.
SCEN.background: The exercise phishing used a newly registered look-alike domain (E6, Appendix A). Brand monitoring, DMARC and patient communication standards are not documented.
SCEN.threat_event: Brand impersonation targeting patients.
vulns: No look-alike domain monitoring or takedown (E6)
No published patient communication standard (e.g. 'we never ask for...')
SCEN.assets: Patient trust; CJ3 patient communications.
SCEN.narrative: Patients receive texts 'MediBec: your results are ready, confirm identity' linking to a copy of the portal. Hundreds enter credentials and health-card numbers; front desks receive angry calls.
sequence: Preparation - look-alike domain and portal clone
Business impact - patient harm, trust erosion

consequences.Confidentiality/privacy: Patient credentials and identifiers stolen outside MediBec.

PbA.rat: Look-alike domain already observed in the exercise.

Pbx.rat: No brand protection evidenced.

SCEN.cvss_note: Limited applicability: impersonation outside MediBec's systems. Representative weakness: sender domain spoofable without enforced DMARC. Business impact is captured by damage estimates, not CVSS.
SCEN.treatment: Look-alike domain monitoring and takedown, verified sender channels, patient communication standard and awareness notices (I23), DMARC enforcement (I16), staff reporting (I12).
SCEN.mapping_note: ATT&CK and CWE links: analyst mapping for the teaching case — validation required.

families.name: Identity takeover of clinical, privileged or cloud-administrator accounts
families.statement: A cybercriminal obtains valid credentials or session tokens for clinic administrators, clinicians or cloud administrators - through EHR-themed phishing, MFA push fatigue, help-desk reset fraud or token theft - and exploits push-only MFA, absent conditional access and weak reset verification to access the EHR, mail and the cloud tenant, leading to health-data exposure and a foothold for destructive attacks.
families.rationale: Most evidenced and most frequent entry path; one identity plane gates every crown jewel. Four variants (phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk reset, token theft) consolidated so the portfolio is not dominated by identity attacks; they share owner (CIO) and treatment family (phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, reset verification).
why: Identity gates every crown jewel and remote/cloud access is central to MediBec's model.
Phishing lure and approved MFA push from unusual geography (E6).
Health-data confidentiality (O2); precursor to O1 disruption.
Push-only MFA, no conditional access, unknown reset verification.
Unauthorized EHR/mail access; reportable breach; ransomware foothold.
Highest likelihood entry path with strongest evidence; variants consolidated.

families.name: Ransomware with data theft and backup destruction halting multi-clinic operations
families.statement: A ransomware affiliate enters through P01 or P03, is not detected because alerts are mis-triaged and logs are incomplete, escalates to domain administrator through Active Directory weaknesses, deletes backups reachable from the production domain, exfiltrates health data and encrypts servers, hypervisors and clinic storage, halting EHR, scheduling and diagnostics across clinics while recovery fails.
families.rationale: Highest combined consequence; full chain visible in exercise; hits several escalation criteria (safety, essential service, backup destruction, primary+recovery failure). Detection gaps, untested IR and backup compromise are stages of this chain, so they are analysed inside it rather than as separate scenarios.
why: Clinics depend on central services; healthcare is a sustained ransomware target.
Full exercise timeline; backup failures; alert closed as low (E6).
Safe continuous care (O1) and all others.
Weak triage, flat network, backups reachable, untested IR.
Multi-clinic outage, data theft, failed recovery.
Largest combined consequence; several mandatory escalation criteria.

families.name: Exploitation of exposed internet-facing systems (unpatched edge devices, admin interfaces, end-of-life systems)
families.statement: A cybercriminal or state-linked actor exploits a known vulnerability in an unpatched VPN or firewall appliance, or default/stuffed credentials on an internet-exposed management interface, because MediBec lacks an attack-surface inventory and timely patching, gaining administrative access to infrastructure and a path to data theft or P02.
families.rationale: Technical entry path distinct from identity (P01): different controls (attack-surface management, patch SLAs), owner (Infrastructure) and velocity (days from disclosure to exploitation). Directly tied to an explicit appetite rule on critical vulnerabilities.
why: Remote access is essential and edge devices are prime targets.
Documented patching constraints (E3, E7); exposure unknown (E4).
O1 and O2 via infrastructure compromise.
Patch lag, unknown exposed interfaces, possible default credentials.
Infrastructure takeover, outage, data access.
Distinct control set and owner; tied to explicit appetite rule on critical vulnerabilities.

families.name: Compromise of connected medical devices disrupting diagnostics and threatening patient safety
families.statement: An attacker or spreading malware reaches a clinic network - via infected workstation, clinic Wi-Fi, patient-supplied imaging media or building IoT - and exploits unpatched or default-credential medical devices sharing that network, disrupting imaging and diagnostic equipment, altering device data and using devices as persistent footholds.
families.rationale: Only scenario where the cyber event directly affects medical equipment; peripheral assets outside IT oversight (instruction s.2-3); certification limits make treatment a distinct management decision. Wi-Fi, media and IoT are entry paths into the same exposure.
why: Medical equipment is interconnected with the EHR environment (E2).
Inventory and segmentation are open questions (E4); certification constraints (E3).
Safe care (O1).
Unpatchable devices on shared networks; peripheral entry paths.
Unavailable or incorrect diagnostics; patient-safety risk.
Only direct safety path through equipment; peripheral assets.

families.name: Manipulation of clinical data (records or interface messages) leading to unsafe care
families.statement: An attacker using a compromised clinical account, a malicious insider, or an attacker positioned on the network alters medication, allergy, laboratory or imaging data - in the EHR or in cleartext HL7/DICOM interface traffic - without detection because integrity monitoring and reconciliation are absent, leading to incorrect clinical decisions.
families.rationale: Low-frequency/high-consequence integrity risk; the portfolio would otherwise treat integrity only as a side effect. Distinct controls (integrity monitoring, reconciliation, interface encryption) and owner (CMO/Clinical Ops).
families.judgment: Retained as a low-frequency, high-consequence patient-safety scenario: without it the portfolio would treat integrity only as a side effect.
why: Clinical decisions rely on EHR, lab and pharmacy data (E1).
Integrity controls listed as expected but absent (E8).
Safe care (O1) and trust (O4).
No integrity monitoring; cleartext interfaces; broad write access.
Wrong treatment; loss of confidence in the record.
Low-frequency/high-consequence; only integrity-centred scenario.

families.name: Misuse of legitimate EHR or service-account access to extract patient records
families.statement: A malicious or curious employee, or an attacker who has taken over the over-privileged ehr-sync-svc service account, uses legitimate but excessive access to query and export patient or billing records, because access is broad, service accounts are not vaulted and EHR access is not monitored, resulting in a privacy breach.
families.rationale: Insider misuse is a recurrent healthcare exposure and is directly evidenced by the service-account anomaly. Distinct from P01 (legitimate access, no perimeter crossing) and P10 (malicious intent); owner is the Privacy officer.
why: EHR access is central and broad; insiders are frequent actors in healthcare.
ehr-sync-svc anomaly (E6); access reviews not evidenced (E7).
Privacy (O2).
Broad roles; un-vaulted service account; no monitoring.
Privacy breach, legal and HR consequences.
Distinct actor and controls from P01/P10; direct evidence.

families.name: Bulk exposure of health data held outside core systems (cloud exports, APIs, clinic storage)
families.statement: An opportunistic actor or intruder obtains bulk patient data from stores that sit outside the EHR's controls - cloud storage used for image transfer shared through long-lived links, API keys leaked from code or configuration, and unmanaged local clinic storage - because posture management, secret management and data minimization are absent, causing a large reportable breach.
families.rationale: Data-at-rest exposure outside the EHR is evidenced (external download of image export) and produces the largest breach volumes. Consolidates three variants that share the treatment decision (data discovery, posture management, minimization) and owner.
why: Image sharing and exports use cloud storage; data spread across clinics.
External download of image export (E6); sprawl question (E4).
Privacy (O2), trust (O4).
Permissive sharing, no posture or secret management, data sprawl.
Large-scale reportable breach.
Largest breach volumes; evidenced; consolidates variants.

families.name: Compromise through a critical supplier (vendor remote access or trojanized software update)
families.statement: A threat actor compromises an EHR, diagnostic, device or IT-support supplier and enters MediBec through the supplier's standing remote access or a malicious signed software update, bypassing perimeter controls, because supplier assurance, contract clauses, access brokering and update staging are absent.
families.rationale: Critical supply-chain concentration is a mandatory escalation criterion; residual stays above tolerance even with funding, so it drives transfer and acceptance decisions rather than spending. Remote-access and update vectors share owner (Procurement/CIO) and the supplier-assurance decision.
why: MediBec relies on EHR, device, cloud and support vendors.
Vendor controls listed only as expectations (E5, E7).
O1 and O2 through trusted paths.
Standing vendor access; no assurance; unstaged updates.
Trusted-path intrusion across many systems.
Mandatory supply-chain concentration criterion; drives transfer decisions.

families.name: Loss of the Montreal hub or WAN isolating all clinics from clinical systems
families.statement: A carrier failure, attack on edge network devices, failure of the single primary firewall pair or data-centre incident takes the Montreal hub offline; because all clinics depend on it without tested redundancy, alternate site or rehearsed downtime procedures, EHR, imaging and pharmacy access is lost network-wide.
families.rationale: Instruction s.3 requires explicit analysis of single points of failure; this is the organization's largest concentration risk and is independent of any attacker, so it is not captured by P02. Distinct decision (redundancy / alternate site investment, IT-funded).
why: All clinics connect through one Montreal hub (E2).
Architecture documented; redundancy not evidenced.
Clinical continuity (O1).
Single hub, possible single carrier/firewall pair, no alternate site.
Network-wide loss of clinical systems.
Largest single point of failure; independent of attackers so not covered by P02.

families.name: Uncontrolled disclosure of patient information by staff through unapproved AI tools and communications
families.statement: Clinicians and administrative staff paste identifiable patient information into public generative-AI or unassessed AI-scribe services, or misdirect e-mails and faxes, because MediBec has no AI acceptable-use policy, sanctioned tool, web/DLP controls or secure referral channel, resulting in systemic uncontrolled disclosure of health information and possible cross-border transfer.
families.rationale: Chosen over the higher-scoring C31 (admin sabotage) for portfolio coverage and decision usefulness: it is the only material negligent-insider and emerging-technology exposure, is near-certain to occur, and drives decisions (AI policy, sanctioned tool, controls) that no other scenario triggers. C31's treatments are largely delivered by P01/P02 controls.
families.judgment: Retained for coverage and decision usefulness: the only negligent-insider and AI exposure, driving a distinct decision on AI policy and sanctioned tools.
why: Clinicians are adopting AI; MediBec pursues governed innovation (E5).
Sector evidence; no MediBec policy documented.
Privacy (O2), governed innovation (O5).
No AI policy, sanctioned tool or controls.
Systemic uncontrolled disclosure; clinical errors.
Only negligent-insider/emerging-tech exposure; unique decisions.

watch.trigger: Consequence bounded and treated by low-cost finance controls; confirm payment-verification procedure with Finance. Promote if procedure is absent and payment volumes are large.

Scores higher than P10 on raw criteria and triggers escalation flags (privileged infrastructure, backup destruction). Excluded because PAM, immutable backup and offboarding controls in P01/P02 treat it; management should confirm this reliance.
Existence of a patient portal is unconfirmed; promote immediately if confirmed.
Look-alike domain observed; harm largely outside MediBec systems; handle through communications and domain monitoring.
Online-service criticality undocumented; revisit if online booking becomes essential.
Not assessed; coordinate with physical security owner.
